content: The guideline will also be relevant to the following groups: National advisory boards on HIV treatment and prevention. Managers of national tuberculosis (TB) programs. Managers of national hepatitis programs. Managers of maternal, newborn, child health, and reproductive health programs. Clinicians and other healthcare providers. Managers of national laboratory services. Individuals living with HIV and community-based organizations. International and bilateral agencies and organizations that provide financial and technical support to HIV programs in resource-limited settings. Guiding Principles 1. The guideline aims to contribute to and accelerate the achievement of global health goals related to HIV and other health priorities for the period 2016–2021. 2. It is based on a public health approach to scaling up the use of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs across the continuum of HIV prevention, treatment, and care. 3. The recommendations should be implemented with the goal of strengthening broader health systems, particularly primary and chronic care services, in addition to improving the continuum of HIV services. 4. Implementation must include efforts to promote and protect the human rights of individuals requiring HIV services. This includes ensuring informed consent, preventing stigma and discrimination, and promoting gender equity. 5. The implementation of the recommendations should be tailored to the local context, taking into account factors such as HIV epidemiology, resource availability, health system capacity, and anticipated cost-effectiveness. Competing Interests All external contributors to the development of this guideline, including members of the Core Group, Clinical Guideline Development Group, and External Review Group, completed a WHO Declaration of Interests form. In line with WHO policy, a brief biography of each Clinical Guideline Development Group member was published on the WHO HIV website for 14 days, along with the meeting objectives. No public comments or objections were received regarding the group membership. The responsible technical officer reviewed all Declaration of Interests forms, and a management plan for each declared conflict was agreed upon and documented. All declared interests and management strategies were discussed with the chairs and methodologist. Conflicts of interest were disclosed at the start of the Clinical Guideline Development Group meeting, and participation was closely monitored by the WHO Guideline Steering Group and GRADE methodologist. Most members of the Clinical Guideline Development Group did not declare significant conflicts of interest for this meeting. Efforts were made to minimize conflicts of interest while ensuring representation of key experts, despite the challenges posed by the involvement of pharmaceutical companies in HIV research and ARV drug trials. The WHO Guideline Steering Group assessed all completed Declaration of Interests forms for other external contributors to the guidelines. Individual participation was reviewed in light of the declared interests. All Declaration of Interests forms are stored electronically at the WHO Department of HIV/AIDS and will be maintained for at least 10 years. Funding for this guideline was provided by grants from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the United States Agency for International Development, the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the United States President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief. Guideline Contributors Three external review teams conducted systematic reviews to support the development of this guideline. Annex 2 provides full details of the team leaders and members. Nandi Siegfried served as the GRADE methodologist for this guideline. An internal Guideline Steering Group, composed of WHO staff and consultants, coordinated the overall guideline development process. Meg Doherty and Rachel Beanland from the Department of HIV/AIDS led the Guideline Steering Group. A Core Group of external experts provided strategic guidance and external review of the guideline. An external Clinical Guideline Development Group, convened by WHO, reviewed evidence and developed the recommendations. The composition of this group adhered to WHO procedures for guideline development and included HIV experts, researchers, program managers, epidemiologists, human rights experts, representatives from United Nations agencies, and civil society organizations, as well as networks of people living with HIV. Civil society representatives were selected through a call for nominations, with three participants chosen from over 90 applications. The WHO HIV Civil Society Reference Group contributed to the selection process, ensuring appropriate representation by region and sex. The Co-Chairs of the Clinical Guideline Development Group also participated in the Core Group to ensure consistency. WHO also recruited an External Review Group of experts in the field to review and provide comments on the guideline. Methods for Evidence Synthesis The WHO Guideline Steering Group formulated PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions to guide systematic reviews for the guideline development. Scoping meetings on HIV treatment among adolescents and the use of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention contributed to this process. Three key PICO questions were identified: 1. In adults, adolescents, and children with HIV, is initiating ART at a CD4 threshold above 500 cells/mm³ compared to below 500 cells/mm³ more harmful? 2. Should pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV who start triple ARV drugs continue lifelong ART regardless of eligibility criteria? 3. Should oral PrEP containing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) be offered as an additional prevention option for individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection as part of combination prevention approaches? No changes were made to the scope of the guideline after the planning proposal was approved. A list of potential outcomes of interest for each question was circulated to all members of the Clinical Guideline Development Group, who scored the importance of each outcome on a scale of 1 (not important) to 9 (critical) from the perspective of individuals living with HIV. The average scores and variability informed decision-making. Systematic review teams developed protocols and conducted reviews in accordance with PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Annex 2 includes search strategies, quality assessments, and synthesis of findings. Qualitative literature reviews supported all three questions. Community consultations were conducted to explore the acceptability of earlier ART initiation, involving 24 workshops in eight countries (India, Indonesia, Kenya, Peru, Portugal, Ukraine, Zambia, and Zimbabwe). Additional consultations on adolescent treatment and care and a facility-based situational analysis contributed to the evidence base. Quality of Evidence and Strength of Recommendations The GRADE method was used to assess the quality of evidence and determine the strength of recommendations. Evidence quality is defined as the confidence that the reported estimates of effect are adequate to support a specific recommendation. The GRADE system classifies evidence quality as high, moderate, low, or very low. Randomized controlled trials are initially rated as high-quality evidence but may be downgraded for reasons such as bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, or publication bias. Observational studies are initially rated as low-quality evidence but may be upgraded if the treatment effect is very large, there is evidence of a dose-response relationship, or all plausible biases would underestimate the effect. The strength of a recommendation reflects the confidence of the Clinical Guideline Development Group that the desirable effects of the recommendation outweigh the undesirable effects. Recommendations can be strong or conditional. A strong recommendation indicates confidence that the desirable effects clearly outweigh the undesirable effects. A conditional recommendation suggests that the desirable effects probably outweigh the undesirable effects, but there is less certainty about these trade-offs in all situations. Decision-Making and Peer Review The Clinical Guideline Development Group made decisions by consensus. Voting was used as a decision-making aid for the question of when to initiate ART for adults, with a majority vote of 70%. A draft of the guideline was circulated for review to members of the Clinical Guideline Development Group, the Core Group, and the External Review Group.
